mus-s2.name: Advanced Functional Harmony: Overtone Series, Inversions, and the Four Cadences
mus-s2.summary: Covers the natural overtone series, the notation of inversions of triads and seventh chords, the tonic-subdominant-dominant (T-S-D) functional harmony system and the four cadences, the eight types of nonchord tones, and secondary seventh chords and modulation.

mus-s3.name: Counterpoint and Musical Form: Fugue and Sonata
mus-s3.summary: Covers 18th-century strict counterpoint and the rules on four-part voice leading (prohibitions on parallel fifths and octaves), imitative counterpoint and the structure of the fugue (Fuga), and the three-part narrative of classical sonata form (exposition, development, recapitulation).

mus-s4.summary: Covers Western music history from Gregorian chant through Baroque basso continuo, the Classical period, and Romanticism, atonal music and twelve-tone technique in the 20th century, and Korean traditional music's twelve lyu-ryeo pitch system, the three-part division by addition and subtraction (samboon-sonik), and the sanjo rhythmic cycles and tori modes.

mus-s5.name: Musical Acoustics, Tuning Systems, and Music Psychology
mus-s5.summary: Covers Pythagorean and just intonation, the Pythagorean comma of twelve-tone equal temperament, the overtone spectrum and timbre of different instruments, and the psychoacoustics of consonance and dissonance and Gestalt perception of music.

mus-s6.name: Bachelor's Capstone: Analysis of Harmony and Form and Arrangement
mus-s6.summary: Comprehensive analysis of the harmonic symbols (Roman numerals), nonchord tones, cadences, and sonata structure of short Classical pieces, followed by arranging and critiquing an 8-bar melodic motif as a four-part functional harmony texture.

mus-01.title: Three Properties of Sound
explain: The material of music is sound. Sound is produced when an object **vibrates**. When you pluck a string, the string vibrates, and that vibration spreads through the air and reaches the ear. This lesson does not play any sound. Instead, you learn to read **waveform** pictures, which show sound as a graph, and to read musical notation.

When distinguishing sounds, music first considers three properties.
- **Pitch**: whether the sound is high or low.
- **Loudness**: whether the sound is loud or soft.
- **Timbre**: the texture of a sound that lets you tell a piano from a violin even when pitch and loudness are the same.

A waveform graph has time on the horizontal axis and the upward and downward size of the vibration on the vertical axis. From this graph you can read each of the three properties.
- Pitch is determined by **how many times it vibrates in the same amount of time** (frequency). The unit for counting vibrations per second is hertz (Hz). In general, the higher the frequency, the higher the sound is heard.
- Loudness is greater when the **width of the vibration** (amplitude) is larger.
- Timbre changes when the **shape of the waveform** is different.

mus-02.title: Basics of Reading a Score
explain: A **score** is a picture that records the pitch and length of sounds with symbols. Pitch is shown by the **vertical position** of the note on the staff, and length is shown by the **shape** of the note.

The background on which notes are placed is the **staff**. It consists of five horizontal lines, which are counted from the bottom up, from the first line to the fifth line. The gaps between the lines are **spaces**, and there are four of them. Notes sit on a line or in a space, and the higher a note sits, the higher its pitch.

The **treble clef** at the start of the staff tells you that the **second line, which the curl of the clef wraps around, is G (sol)**. The names of the other notes are determined from this line. Note names repeat the seven letters C D E F G A B. In C major, do-re-mi-fa-sol-la-ti correspond in order to C D E F G A B.

On the staff, the notes on the lines are, from the bottom, **E G B D F**, and the notes in the spaces are, from the bottom, **F A C E**. Notes outside the staff are written with short extra lines called **ledger lines**. The C on a ledger line just below the first line is commonly called **middle C**. Because the same name appears at many heights, people sometimes add a number to tell them apart, such as C4 for middle C and C5 one octave above.

body: Silent intervals are also written in the score. These are **rests**, and they have the same names and lengths as notes. A whole rest is 4 beats of silence, a half rest 2 beats, a quarter rest 1 beat, and an eighth rest half a beat.

mus-03.title: Scales: Whole Steps and Half Steps
explain: A **scale** is a set of notes stacked in order of rising pitch. The smallest unit for measuring the interval between notes is the **half step**. On the keyboard, the space between **two neighboring keys** (including the black keys) is a half step. An interval of **two** half steps is a **whole step**.

explain.alt: A picture of one octave of keys. Eight white keys are labeled from the bottom C D E F G A B C and do re mi fa sol la ti do. Black keys lie between C and D, D and E, F and G, G and A, and A and B. There are no black keys between E and F or between B and the high C, and an orange triangle with the words 'no black key' points to those places.
explain.caption: Among the white keys, only E and F and B and the high C have no black key between them.

explain: On the keyboard, there is one black key between C and D. From C to the black key is one half step, and from the black key to D is another half step, so C and D form a whole step. By contrast, E and F, and B and C, have their keys directly next to each other, so they are a **half step** apart.

A **major scale** is a scale in which whole steps and half steps are stacked in a fixed order. From bottom to top the pattern is **whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half**. The major scale of C major starts on C and climbs **do re mi fa sol la ti do** in order, and this structure is produced by the white keys alone. The half steps fall between mi and fa, and between ti and the high do.

Even if you change the starting note, you still get a major scale as long as the same whole-step and half-step order is kept. To do so, the white keys alone are not enough, and black keys become necessary. This lesson deals only with C major.

mus-04.title: Beat and Rhythm
explain: **Rhythm** is the flow created by the alternation of long and short sounds. Underneath rhythm lies a steady series of **beats**. Beats are counted evenly, like the steps of walking. Each section that the beats are grouped into by vertical lines (**bar lines**) is a **measure**.

The **time signature** is the pair of numbers written like a fraction at the very start of the staff. The top number tells you **how many beats are in one measure**, and the bottom number tells you **which note value is counted as one beat**. When the bottom number is 4, the quarter note is one beat.
- **4/4**: one measure holds the value of four quarter notes.
- **3/4**: one measure holds the value of three quarter notes.
- **2/4**: one measure holds the value of two quarter notes.

explain.alt: Three staves each show a time signature and quarter notes. The first has 4 over 4 with four quarter notes, the second has 3 over 4 with three quarter notes, and the third has 2 over 4 with two quarter notes. Beneath them is written: one measure of 4 beats, one measure of 3 beats, and one measure of 2 beats.
explain.caption: The number on top tells you how many quarter notes fill a measure.

explain: The total length of all the notes and rests in each measure, **when added together, must equal the number of beats the time signature sets**. A 4/4 measure has 4 beats. A half note (2 beats) plus two quarter notes (1 beat + 1 beat) is 4 beats, which fills the measure. An eighth note is half a beat, so two of them together make 1 beat.

There are two more ways to adjust the length of notes. A **tie** joins two notes of the same pitch with a curved line, and they are sounded as **one sound** whose length is the sum of the two. A **dotted note** has a dot placed to the right of it, which adds **half of its original length**. A dotted quarter note is 1 + 1/2 = 1 and 1/2 beats.

body: A adds up to 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 beats, so it is full. B is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 beats, so it is one beat short. C is four eighth notes (2 beats) plus a half note (2 beats), which adds up to 4 beats.
A short measure can be filled with a rest. Adding a quarter rest at the end of measure B makes it 4 beats.

mus-05.title: Chords and Tonality
explain: A **chord** is two or more notes that sound **simultaneously**. The most basic chord is the **triad**, which is made by stacking three notes, skipping one note at a time. From the bottom, they are called the **root, third, and fifth**. Counting the root as 1, the third note is the third and the fifth note is the fifth.
On the staff, the notes of a triad are stacked either **all on lines** or **all in spaces**, because each stacked note skips one line or space.

explain.alt: Three triads, each with three notes stacked upward on a treble-clef staff. The first, with notes on the ledger line below the staff, the first line, and the second line, is labeled I, tonic triad, C E G, and is tagged from the bottom as root, third, and fifth. The second, with notes in the first, second, and third spaces, is IV, subdominant triad, F A C. The third, with notes on the second, third, and fourth lines, is V, dominant triad, G B D.
explain.caption: The three triads of C major. They are built upward from the root through the third to the fifth.

explain: In C major, a chord built upward from do is do-mi-sol (C-E-G). This chord is the **tonic triad**, the stable chord at the center of the key. The chord built from fa, fa-la-do (F-A-C), is the **subdominant triad**, and the chord built from sol, sol-ti-re (G-B-D), is the **dominant triad**. The tonic triad is usually written with the Roman numeral I, the subdominant triad with IV, and the dominant triad with V.

**Tonality** is an order in which one note (the tonic) serves as the center, and the remaining notes and chords are arranged in relation to that center. In C major, C is the center. The tonic triad is often described as sounding like a place of rest, and the dominant triad as sounding like a place that wants to return to the tonic triad.

There are two kinds of triads with different sound qualities. A **major triad** has 4 half steps from the root to the third and 3 half steps from the third to the fifth. A **minor triad** is the reverse, with 3 half steps followed by 4. In general, the major triad is said to sound bright and firm, and the minor triad dark and subdued, but the feeling can differ depending on the listener and the context of the music.

examples.title: Measuring the intervals of C-E-G
body: From do to mi is do-re (a whole step, 2 half steps) and re-mi (a whole step, 2 half steps), so it is 4 half steps. From mi to sol is mi-fa (1 half step) and fa-sol (a whole step, 2 half steps), so it is 3 half steps. Since it is 4 and then 3, do-mi-sol is a major triad.
By the same method, la-do-mi (from la to do is 3 half steps, and from do to mi is 4) is a minor triad.

mus-06.title: Musical Form and How to Listen to It
explain: A piece may seem to flow in a single line, but it is usually divided into several **sections**. The pattern in which sections repeat or new ones appear is the **form**. Identical sections are labeled with the same letter. The first section is called **A**, and a new section that clearly contrasts with what came before is called **B**.

There are three typical patterns.
- **One-part form (A)**: one section, repeated if needed.
- **Two-part form (A-B)**: a new section follows the first section.
- **Three-part form (A-B-A)**: the first section, a contrasting section, and then the first section returns.

explain.alt: A diagram of boxes in three rows. The one-part row has one A box, the two-part row has an A box followed by a B box, and the three-part row has A, B, and A boxes in order. Beneath them is an arrow showing that time flows to the right.
explain.caption: The same letter means that the same melody returns.

explain: The way to hear form comes down to two questions. **Is the melody being played now one that you heard earlier?** If so, it has the same letter; if not, it has a new letter. Asking this question each time the section changes draws a map of the piece.

The sound of a piece played by several performers is described by **instrument families**. There are many ways to classify instruments, and here we use common categories.
- **Strings**: sound is produced by bowing or plucking strings. (violin, cello)
- **Woodwinds**: sound is produced by blowing air into a tube. (clarinet)
- **Brass**: sound is produced by buzzing the lips and blowing into a metal tube. (trumpet, trombone)
- **Percussion**: sound is produced by striking or shaking. (bass drum)

mus-07.title: Functional Harmony: The Natural Harmonic Series and Inversions of Triads and Seventh Chords
explain: The tonic triad of C major (C-E-G, do-mi-sol), which people find the most comfortable in music, is not a chord that humans arbitrarily invented. It is a gift of nature that arises from the physical overtone (Harmonics) structure contained in all natural sounds. When a string or an air column vibrates, sounds that vibrate at whole-number multiples of the basic frequency (2 times, 3 times, 4 times, and so on) sound together with it. These are called the **natural harmonic series** (Harmonic Series).

explain.alt: A diagram of the natural harmonic series for overtones 1 through 8, based on the fundamental C2. Overtone 1, C2 (65 Hz); overtone 2, C3 (perfect octave); overtone 3, G3 (perfect fifth); overtone 4, C4 (perfect fourth); overtone 5, E4 (major third); overtone 6, G4 (minor third); overtone 7, Bb4; and overtone 8, C5, are each shown in order as dots on the staff.

explain: Let us look at the harmonic series in the diagram above. Overtone 2 (C) forms a perfect octave with overtone 1 (1:2), overtone 3 (G) forms a perfect fifth with overtone 2 (2:3), overtone 4 (C) forms a perfect fourth with overtone 3 (3:4), and overtone 5 (E) forms a major third with overtone 4 (4:5). Collecting overtones 4, 5, and 6 gives exactly C-E-G (do-mi-sol), so a complete **major triad** forms naturally. Western harmony has developed over several centuries on the basis of the whole-number consonant relationships of this harmonic series.

When the bass is the lowest note of a chord's voices, the character of the chord changes depending on which note is in the bass. This is called **inversion**, and it is written in traditional figured bass notation.
- **Triad inversions**:
  - Root position: the root is in the bass, a 5/3 chord (usually omitted).
  - First inversion: the third is in the bass (for example, in do-mi-sol, mi is the lowest note), a 6/3 chord (symbol **$I^6$**). It connects smoothly with a melodic bass line.
  - Second inversion: the fifth is in the bass (sol is the lowest note), **$I^6_4$ six-four chord**. Because it forms a dissonant fourth with the bass, it is very unstable, and it is strictly limited to the cadential six-four (Cadential 6/4) just before a cadence or to passing use.
- **Seventh-chord inversions**:
  - Root position $V^7$, first inversion (third in the bass) **$V^6_5$**, second inversion (fifth in the bass) **$V^4_3$**, third inversion (seventh in the bass) **$V^4_2$** (or $V^2$).

Limitation: the 7th harmonic (Bb) is about 31 cents lower than the equal-tempered minor seventh, and the 11th harmonic lies between the perfect fourth and the augmented fourth, so it sounds like a dissonance. Therefore, music uses the natural harmonic series as its foundation but corrects it with artificial scales and tuning systems.

examples.title: Identifying the inversion of the I chord in C major
body: Condition: In a four-part choral texture, the soprano is on sol, the alto on do, the tenor on do, and the bass on mi.
Step 1: The chord tones are do-mi-sol (a C major triad).
Step 2: The lowest note, the bass, is the third, 'mi (E)', so this is the first inversion.
Interpretation: In Roman numeral analysis it is written $I^6$, and it helps the bass line move smoothly.

examples.title: Resolution of the cadential six-four (Cadential 6/4)
body: Condition: Just before the end of the piece, the bass is held on sol (G), and the six-four chord $I^6_4$ appears.
Step 1: The sixth (mi) and the fourth (do) above the bass in $I^6_4$ (do-mi-sol with sol in the bass) have a dissonant character.
Step 2: As mi steps down to re (the fifth) and do steps down to ti (the third), the chord changes to the $V$ chord (sol-ti-re), and finally closes on $I$.
Interpretation: The six-four chord is not an independent tonic triad. It has a decorative role that modifies and delays the dominant chord ($V$).

checks.prompt: Match each inversion of a chord with its figured bass analysis symbol.
checks.hint: Check the first inversion of a triad (6), the second inversion (6/4), the first inversion of a seventh chord (6/5), and the third inversion (4/2).
checks.explanation: This is the figured bass notation system for chord inversions in classical functional harmony.
pairs: I⁶ (bass is the third; intervals of sixth and third)
I⁶₄ (bass is the fifth; intervals of sixth and fourth)
V⁶₅ (bass is the third; intervals of sixth and fifth)
V⁴₂ or V² (bass is the seventh; intervals of fourth and second)

checks.prompt: Which kind of chord forms naturally when the 4th (C4), 5th (E4), and 6th (G4) harmonics of the natural harmonic series sound together?
checks.hint: Do-mi-sol is a bright, consonant major triad.
checks.explanation: The frequency ratio 4:5:6 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th harmonics is the perfect physical prototype of a natural major triad.

checks.hint: In counterpoint, the perfect fourth above the bass is treated as a dissonance.
checks.explanation: The fourth between the bass and the upper note creates tension, so it must be resolved, for example by a cadential six-four.

Because it is too difficult for the performer to press the keys

mus-08.title: Functional Harmony: The T-S-D Functional Cycle and the Four Cadences
explain: In tonal music, chords are not arranged at random. The nineteenth-century German music theorist Hugo Riemann integrated all diatonic chords into three fundamental musical functions: **Tonic (T) - Subdominant (S) - Dominant (D)**.

explain.alt: A diagram of the functional harmony system and the structure of the four cadences. It shows a cycle in which the tonic (I, vi; stable) moves through the subdominant (IV, ii; departure) to the dominant (V, vii°; maximum tension), and the dominant resolves back to the tonic. Below it, the four types of cadence (authentic, plagal, half, and deceptive) are summarized.

explain:
1. **Energy cycle of the T-S-D functional system**:
- **Tonic (T, tonic triad group: I, vi)**: a state of perfect stability and rest, like home.
- **Subdominant (S, subdominant triad group: IV, ii)**: a stage of departure and leap out of stability, preparing tension and setting out on a new journey.
- **Dominant (D, dominant triad group: V, vii°)**: contains the leading tone (leading tone, ti$\rightarrow$do) that is pulled strongly toward the tonic, and is an unstable state in which musical tension reaches its peak.
The basic principle of progression is the cycle **T $\rightarrow$ S $\rightarrow$ D $\rightarrow$ T**. The subdominant readily moves to the dominant, but moving backward from the dominant to the subdominant (D $\rightarrow$ S) is in principle forbidden in the classical style.

2. **The four cadences (Cadence)**:
These are the harmonic knots that close a phrase or a piece.
- **Authentic cadence (Authentic Cadence, V $\rightarrow$ I)**: the most complete ending, resolving from the dominant to the tonic. If both the soprano and bass end on the root and V is in root position, it is called a perfect authentic cadence (PAC); otherwise it is called an imperfect authentic cadence (IAC).
- **Plagal cadence (Plagal Cadence, IV $\rightarrow$ I)**: used for the 'Amen' at the end of hymns, and so also called the **amen cadence**. Added after an authentic cadence, it leaves a soft and majestic afterglow.
- **Half cadence (Half Cadence, ? $\rightarrow$ V)**: no matter which chord it starts from, it stops on the dominant (V) with a rest or a fermata. It is not a musical period but throws out a question mark (?) that passes the narrative on to the next phrase.
- **Deceptive cadence (Deceptive Cadence, V $\rightarrow$ vi)**: after the dominant (V), the audience expects the tonic (I) with near certainty, but the music defies that expectation by detouring to the submediant chord (vi). By betraying expectation, it does not halt the music but dramatically extends the narrative.

Limitation: the T-S-D functional harmony system explains the Classical and early Romantic periods perfectly, but after Wagner in the late nineteenth century, in chromatic harmony, and in the four-chord endless loop (I-V-vi-IV) of postmodern pop music, the hierarchy of functional tension and resolution weakens.

examples.title: Analyzing the conditions of a perfect authentic cadence (PAC)
body: Condition: Analysis of the final cadence measure of a piece in C major.
Step 1: Progress from the $V$ chord (G) to the $I$ chord (C) (D -> T).
Step 2: In both chords the root is in the bass (root position), and the highest soprano note ends on the tonic, 'do (C)'.
Interpretation: Because all three conditions are satisfied, this is the most complete and conclusive perfect authentic cadence (PAC), beyond any doubt.

examples.title: The dramatic effect of the deceptive cadence
body: Condition: In a solemn symphony, the entire orchestra raises tension strongly on the $V^7$ chord.
Step 1: The audience expects it to resolve to the joyful C major $I$ chord.
Step 2: The chord the conductor strikes is A minor, the vi chord with a minor feeling.
Interpretation: By delaying the resolution and throwing out a dark question, the development of the piece is dramatically extended by more than 20 measures.

checks.prompt: Match each cadence in the four cadences with its harmonic progression and musical character.
checks.hint: Check the progressions V-I, IV-I, ?-V, and V-vi.
checks.explanation: These are the standard definitions of the four cadences that close tonal music.
pairs: V → I (the most firm closing from dominant to tonic)
IV → I (the soft amen cadence from subdominant to tonic)
? → V (a question-mark cadence that stops on the dominant and leads to the next phrase)
V → vi (detours to the sixth degree instead of the expected tonic, defying expectation)

checks.prompt: In the T-S-D functional system, which most decisive pitch-based factor draws the dominant (D), at its peak of tension, strongly into the stable tonic (T)?
checks.hint: The leading tone (ti) has a half-step pull toward the tonic (do).
checks.explanation: The half-step resolving drive of the leading tone and the resolution of the tritone in the seventh chord are the source of the dominant's resolution.
options: Because the dominant (V) contains the leading tone (7th degree), which has a strong tendency to rise a half step and resolve to the tonic (1st degree)
Because all the instruments stop breathing at the same moment
Because the orchestral score comes to an end
Because of the weight of the conductor's baton

checks.prompt: Which progression, which goes against the natural cycle of energy in classical functional harmony (T -> S -> D -> T), is in principle avoided?
checks.hint: It is a progression that goes backward from the greatest tension (D) to the preparation of tension (S).
checks.explanation: In the classical style, D → S is regarded as harmonic energy flowing backward, so it is in principle avoided.
options: Retrograde from dominant to subdominant (D → S, e.g., V → IV)
Progression from tonic to subdominant (T → S)
Progression from subdominant to dominant (S → D)
Resolution from dominant to tonic (D → T)

checks.prompt: Which minor triad built on the second degree, belonging to the same family, can fully stand in for the role of the subdominant (IV)?
checks.hint: It is the second-degree chord (re-fa-la) that shares common tones (fa, la) with the fourth-degree chord (fa-la-do).
checks.explanation: The ii chord is the most representative substitute chord, performing the same subdominant function as the IV chord.

mus-09.title: Functional Harmony: Non-Harmonic Tones, Secondary Dominant Seventh Chords, and Modulation
explain: A beautiful melody is not made of chord tones alone. The decorative tones that move among the framework of chords and give tension and color are called **non-harmonic tones** (Non-Harmonic Tones). Non-harmonic tones are strictly classified according to how they are approached (Approach) and how they are resolved (Resolve).

The grammar of the eight types of non-harmonic tones:
1. **Passing tone (Passing Tone)**: a tone that connects two chord tones by passing stepwise between them, without leaps.
2. **Neighbor tone (Neighbor Tone)**: a tone that briefly moves a second above or below a chord tone and then returns to the original note.
3. **Suspension (Suspension)**: when a chord tone of the previous chord carries over into the next chord, it does not resolve right away but 'stays and holds on' (preparation-suspension), then falls a second down late to resolve. It is the most dramatic technique for delaying emotion (e.g., 4-3 suspension, 7-6 suspension).
4. **Appoggiatura (Appoggiatura)**: a romantic accent tone that leaps up a large interval of a third or more on a strong beat, then resolves stepwise a second down.
5. **Escape tone (Escape Tone)**: a tone that moves stepwise away and then resolves by leaping in the opposite direction.
6. **Anticipation (Anticipation)**: a tone in which a note of the next chord appears a moment early, one step ahead of the beat.
7. **Pedal point (Pedal Point)**: a technique in which a single note in the bass (mostly the tonic or dominant) sustains majestically for several measures while the upper-voice chords change freely above it.

The **secondary dominant seventh chord** (Secondary Dominant Chord), which maximizes the color of harmony:
Within C major, this is a technique in which a diatonic chord other than the tonic chord ($I$) (for example, the G chord, which is $V$) is temporarily treated as a 'false tonic', and the dominant seventh chord belonging to it is borrowed and attached in front of it. It is written as **$V^7 / V$** (dominant of the dominant, the D7 chord). At this point, accidentals (sharp or flat) inevitably appear, giving a thrilling harmonic sensation.

**Modulation** (key change), in which the key changes completely:
The most elegant modulation is the **common-chord modulation** (pivot chord modulation), which passes through a bridge chord that the two keys share. For example, when moving from C major to G major, 'A minor', which is the vi chord of C major and the ii chord of G major, serves as the pivot (stepping stone) to switch the key naturally.

Limitation: overusing non-harmonic tones and secondary chords can blur the central gravity of the original key and collapse the tonality. Late Romantic composers pushed these techniques to their limits, which eventually led to the atonal music of the twentieth century.

examples.title: The three-step mechanism of the suspension (Suspension)
body: Condition: In C major, a 4-3 suspension occurs in the progression IV -> V.
Step 1 (preparation, Preparation): In the IV chord (fa-la-do), the soprano's 'do' sounds as a normal chord tone.
Step 2 (suspension, Suspension): The chord changes to V (sol-ti-re), but the soprano keeps holding 'do', forming a dissonant fourth with the bass sol.
Step 3 (resolution, Resolution): After the taut tension, the soprano falls a half step to 'ti' (the third of V) and resolves to a complete chord.
Interpretation: The three stages of preparation, suspension, and resolution produce the sublime pleasure of delaying and releasing emotion.

examples.title: Analysis of the secondary dominant seventh chord V7/V
body: Condition: In a score in C major, a D7 chord (re-fa#-la-do, $D^7$) suddenly appears, followed by a G chord (sol-ti-re, $G$).
Step 1: C major naturally has no fa# (F#). F# is an accidental.
Step 2: D7 is the dominant seventh chord ($V^7$) of G major. The G chord is the $V$ chord of C major.
Interpretation: Therefore this D7 chord is the $V^7/V$ secondary dominant seventh chord, temporarily borrowed to modify the V chord of C major.

checks.prompt: Match each type of non-harmonic tone with its characteristic motion.
checks.hint: Connect stepwise passage, return, delayed descending resolution, and sustained bass.
checks.explanation: These are the definitions of the representative non-harmonic tones that decorate a melody.
pairs: Passes stepwise in one direction between two chord tones
Moves a second above or below a chord tone and returns to the original note
The previous chord tone extends into the next chord, forms a dissonance, then resolves by falling
The chords above change while a single bass note is held

checks.prompt: In C major, to emphasize the dominant G chord (V), a D7 chord (re-fa#-la-do) is borrowed and placed in front of it, treating the G chord as a temporary tonic. What is the harmonic name of this chord?
checks.hint: Secondary dominant (the V7 of V).
checks.explanation: A chord that borrows the dominant seventh chord of a target chord and adds accidentals and tension is called a secondary dominant seventh chord.
options: Cadential chord of the deceptive cadence

checks.prompt: When modulating to a new, different key, which technique transitions by using a chord that belongs to both the original key and the target key as a stepping stone (pivot)?
checks.hint: Use a chord common to both keys as the pivot.
checks.explanation: This is the technique of changing key most smoothly and naturally through a chord shared by the two keys.

checks.prompt: What is the strict three-step progression that a suspension must go through to be established?
checks.hint: It is prepared in the previous chord, held so that it forms a dissonance, and resolves by stepwise descent.
checks.explanation: A suspension always goes through three stages: preparation in the previous chord, the suspension held as a dissonance, and stepwise resolution.

checks.prompt: In two or three sentences, describe the aesthetic effects that non-harmonic tones and secondary dominant chords have on the melody and harmony of classical tonal music.
checks.hint: Describe non-harmonic tones (melodic decoration and tension-resolution) and secondary chords (accidental color and goal-directedness).
checks.explanation: Non-harmonic tones and secondary chords are the key techniques that give tension and color to a monotonous harmony.
checks.model: Non-harmonic tones give the melody smooth connections and the pleasure of tension and resolution through momentary dissonance. When secondary dominant seventh chords are combined with them, the harmonic color grows richer through accidentals, and the drive toward the target chord is maximized, completing a dramatic harmonic narrative.

mus-10.title: Counterpoint and Form I: Eighteenth-Century Counterpoint and Rules of Voice Leading
explain: While harmony studies the 'pillars of chords' that stack vertically over time, **counterpoint** deals with 'a dialogue among several independent melodies' that flow horizontally across time and space. The term derives from the Latin 'punctus contra punctum' (point against point, note against note).

The ultimate ideal of counterpoint is **'each voice possesses its own independent rhythm and melodic vitality, yet when combined vertically they form perfect consonance'**. The reason Johann Sebastian Bach's music is called a monument of human intellect lies precisely in the perfect fusion of this horizontal counterpoint and vertical harmonic quality.

The four types of voice leading (Voice Leading):
1. **Parallel motion (Parallel Motion)**: two voices move in the same direction while maintaining the same interval.
2. **Similar motion (Similar Motion)**: two voices move in the same direction, but the intervals between them change.
3. **Contrary motion (Contrary Motion)**: one voice rises while the other falls, moving in opposite directions (the best and most recommended independent progression in counterpoint).
4. **Oblique motion (Oblique Motion)**: one voice stays in place while the other moves.

The absolute prohibition in voice leading: **prohibition of parallel fifths and parallel octaves (Consecutive Fifths and Octaves)**:
Classical counterpoint strictly forbids two voices moving side by side while keeping a perfect fifth or perfect octave. Because the perfect consonances of the fifth and octave fuse so completely in sound, the moment they move in parallel, the two independent voices are absorbed into a single voice, and the **'independence of voices' (Independence of Voices) is completely lost**.
Prohibition of voice crossing (Voice Crossing): when the alto goes higher than the soprano, or the tenor goes lower than the bass, the clear outline of each voice is damaged, so it should be avoided.

examples.title: Identifying a violation of the parallel fifths prohibition
body: Condition: When the bass moves up from C to D, the tenor moves up from G to A.
Step 1: In the first chord, the bass C and the tenor G form a perfect fifth.
Step 2: In the second chord, the bass D and the tenor A also form a perfect fifth.

Interpretation: Because the two voices moved up side by side while keeping a perfect fifth, this is a fatal 'parallel fifths' error. As the solution, the tenor should move down in the opposite direction (contrary motion).

examples.title: The aesthetics of contrary motion
body: Condition: The soprano moves up do-re-mi.
Step 1: Instead of moving the bass up in the same way, the bass moves down mi-re-do.
Step 2: The two voices spread apart in opposite directions like a mirror, and their melodic lines contrast clearly.
Interpretation: Contrary motion is the golden rule of counterpoint that maximizes the independence of each voice.

checks.prompt: In classical counterpoint and four-part harmony, what is the fundamental musical reason for strictly prohibiting parallel fifths and parallel octaves?
checks.hint: The two voices merge into one, and their independence disappears.
checks.explanation: Parallel motion of fifths and octaves erases the independent melodic outline of each voice, violating the great principle of counterpoint.
options: Because when the perfect consonances of the fifth and octave move side by side, the sounds of the two voices merge into one and each voice's own 'independence' is destroyed
Because the performer's fingers cramp up
Because the piano tuning goes out of tune
Because the volume drops to 0 decibels

checks.prompt: Match the directions and characteristics of voice leading.
checks.hint: Connect opposite directions, one voice staying still, the same interval moving in the same direction, and different intervals moving in the same direction.
checks.explanation: These are the four basic types of voice leading in counterpoint.
pairs: One voice rises and the other falls, maximizing voice independence
One voice stays and only the other moves
Two voices move in the same direction while keeping the same interval
Two voices move in the same direction, but the interval between them changes

checks.prompt: Which ideal type of voice leading is most encouraged in counterpoint to preserve the outline of the melodies and the independence of the voices?
checks.hint: Contrary motion, in which the voices move in opposite directions.
checks.explanation: In contrary motion, the directions of the two melodies contrast, so the independence of each voice is most clearly preserved.

checks.prompt: List in order the steps for composing a counter-melody above a given cantus firmus.
checks.hint: Confirm the cantus firmus, then the vertical consonance framework, then contrary or oblique design while avoiding prohibitions, then melodic completion with non-harmonic tones.
checks.explanation: This is the counterpoint compositional process that proceeds from identifying the cantus firmus, to the consonance skeleton, to checking prohibitions, to melodic decoration.
items: Check the pitch of each measure and the position of the cadence in the given cantus firmus
Place the framework on the first beat of each measure, mainly with imperfect consonances such as thirds and sixths
Design the directions of motion between voices as contrary or oblique motion to avoid parallel fifths and octaves
Complete a smooth horizontal melody using non-harmonic tones such as passing tones and neighbor tones

mus-11.title: Counterpoint and Form II: Imitative Counterpoint and the Structure of the Fugue
explain: When one voice begins to sing an attractive melody, and after a moment another voice enters, copying that melody and following it, this musical dialogue is called **imitative counterpoint**. The peak of this imitation, and the flower of contrapuntal music, is the **fugue** (Fuga), which Bach brought to completion.

The core components of the fugue:
1. **Subject** (dux): the core melodic motif in the home key that becomes the genetic material of the whole piece.
2. **Answer**: a melody in which another voice responds by imitating the subject in the dominant key (a fifth above or a fourth below). It is divided into the 'real answer' (Real answer), which exactly copies the interval pattern of the original subject, and the 'tonal answer' (Tonal answer), in which the tonic-dominant intervals are slightly adjusted to keep the harmony of the key.
3. **Countersubject**: an independent secondary melody that the voice that has just finished the subject plays while the answer sounds, accompanying the answer harmonically from above or below.

The architectural structure of the fugue:
- **Exposition**: the entrance in which all voices (soprano, alto, tenor, bass) enter in turn, singing 'subject $\rightarrow$ answer $\rightarrow$ subject $\rightarrow$ answer' one after another like a round.
- **Episode**: after the entrance of all voices is complete, a flexible bridge section in which small fragments of the subject are developed motivically while modulating to a new key.
- **Middle development**: subjects modulated to minor or related keys reappear in various voices.
- **Stretto**: a climactic technique of tension in which one voice's subject has not yet ended before another voice hurriedly bites into the subject and enters, so the two sound overlapped.
- **Organ point** (Organ Point / Pedal Point): while the bass sustains the tonic or dominant majestically, all voices converge solemnly toward the closing section.

Limitation: the fugue demands a high degree of mathematical intellect and architectural precision, and it was criticized for blocking the free outpouring of emotion. Because of this, as the late eighteenth-century Classical era arrived, mainstream status passed to homophony, in which a single melody is carried by harmonic accompaniment, and to sonata form.

examples.title: The order of entrances in the exposition of a fugue from Bach's 'The Well-Tempered Clavier'
body: Condition: a four-voice fugue in C major.
Step 1: The soprano alone plays the 'subject' in C major as a solo.
Step 2: When the alto sings the 'answer' in G major, the soprano accompanies with a 'countersubject'.
Step 3: The tenor comes back in with the 'subject' in C major, and the bass enters with the 'answer' in G major, completing the four-voice exposition.
Interpretation: The voices pile up layer by layer and complete a seamless contrapuntal fabric.

examples.title: The tension-building principle of stretto
body: Condition: there is a long subject that lasts four measures.
Step 1: Normally, one voice sings all four measures before the next voice enters.
Step 2: In the stretto section in the latter part of the piece, after only one measure has been sung, the next voice hurriedly enters with the same subject.
Interpretation: The subject melodies overlap, chasing each other's tails, leaving no time to breathe, and the tension of the climax explodes.

mus-12.title: Counterpoint and Form III: The Drama of Classical Sonata Form
explain: The first movements of the symphonies, string quartets, concertos, and solo sonatas completed by the great Viennese Classical masters of the late eighteenth century, Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven, were without exception built on the monumental architectural framework of **Sonata Form**. Sonata form is not merely a musical frame; it is the **dialectical completion of a human drama**, in which two different characters and keys clash and conflict before finally merging into one.

explain.alt: A diagram of the three-part narrative of classical sonata form. On the left, the exposition: the first theme in I (home key), a transition that modulates, and the second theme in V (dominant key). In the center, the development: motivic breakdown, frequent modulation, dramatic conflict, and a dominant pedal. On the right, the recapitulation: the first theme in I (home key), the second theme brought into the home key I, and the coda, arranged in order.

explain:
The three core sections of sonata form and its key drama:
1. **Exposition**:
- **First theme**: the stately, rhythmic, and masculine theme in the **home key (I)** that opens the piece.
- **Transition**: a bridge role that shakes the key and modulates to the dominant key.
- **Second theme**: in a major-key piece it appears in the **dominant key (V)**; in a minor-key piece it appears in the relative major (III). It has a gentle, lyrical, feminine character in sharp contrast with the first theme. This opposition of the two themes in **different keys (I vs V)** is the starting point of the sonata drama.
- **Codetta**: closes the exposition and is repeated.

2. **Development**:
The motives of the two themes of the exposition are finely divided (fragmented), and frequent modulations crossing related keys and minor keys are undertaken. It is the furnace of the narrative in which the two themes clash fiercely, and the highest dramatic tension section. At the end, a 'dominant pedal' (a sustained dominant note) is laid down to prepare the return to the tonic.

3. **Recapitulation**:
The themes of the exposition return. Here the greatest miracle of sonata form occurs. The first theme comes back in its original form in the home key (I), while the **second theme, which had rebelled by moving to the dominant key in the exposition, now changes its key to the home key (I) and submits and returns**! This is called **'tonal reconciliation' (Tonal Reconciliation)**, in which two dissimilar entities achieve harmony within a single key, and the piece ends in the joy of the **Coda (Coda, closing section)**.

Limitation: sonata form possesses such perfect organic unity that for the Romantic composers of the nineteenth century it became a vast shackle to be surpassed. Liszt's single-movement sonata and Mahler's symphonies dismantled the norms of sonata form and freely unfolded literary narratives.

examples.title: Sonata form in the first movement of Beethoven's Symphony No. 5 ('Fate')
body: Exposition: the rough first theme in C minor (the "fate motif," ta-ta-ta-tam) stands in tonal opposition to the soft, warm second theme in E-flat major.
Development: the fate motif is broken apart and distributed across all sections of the orchestra, roaring in a desperate struggle.
Recapitulation: after the first theme roars out in C minor, the second theme also surrenders and reconciles in C major (the same tonic), and the piece closes with a massive coda.
Interpretation: The conflict and opposition of keys, and the narrative of unity, show the essence of the classical sonata.

examples.title: Identifying the key change of the second theme in the recapitulation
body: Condition: a sonata piece that begins in G major (I).
Step 1: In the exposition, the second theme appears in D major (V), a fifth above.
Step 2: In the recapitulation, the second theme is played not in D major but necessarily in G major (I), the home key.
Interpretation: This is the absolute principle of sonata form, recovering the centrifugal force (departure) of the exposition through the centripetal force (convergence on the home key).

mus-13.title: Music History of the West: From Gregorian Chant to the Classical and Romantic Periods
explain: The thousand-year history of Western art music is a great history of stylistic change, moving from **monophony, a single melodic line, to complex polyphony, then through clear homophony to the explosion of subjective emotion in Romanticism**.

1. **Middle Ages (CE to the 14th century)**: the starting point is **Gregorian chant** (Gregorian Chant), the unaccompanied Latin monophonic chant of the Roman Catholic Church. It was monophony, in which a single melody is sung without accompaniment, and it was based on the eight church modes (Church Modes). In the twelfth century, with the Notre-Dame school of Paris (Léonin, Pérotin), the first polyphonic music, called organum (Organum), began to sprout.
2. **Renaissance (15th to 16th centuries)**: together with humanism centered on people, the Netherlands school and Palestrina's **imitative contrapuntal polyphony (Polyphony)** blossomed. Four to six voices intertwined like rolling waves on equal footing, creating a heavenly harmony.

3. **Baroque (1600–1750)**: an age of dramatic contrast of light and dark and of emotional expression (ethos). Around 1600 the first opera was born in Italy, and **basso continuo** (Basso Continuo), in which an organ or harpsichord fills in harmony over a sustained bass line, dominated all genres. Vivaldi's concertos (Concerto), Bach's fugues and passions, and Handel's oratorios were the peaks of the Baroque.
4. **Classical period (1750–1820)**: the era of the Viennese Classical school (Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven), grounded in the reason of the Enlightenment. Shedding the difficulty of polyphony, it established **homophony** (Homophony), in which one beautiful melody is accompanied by harmony, along with balanced four-measure phrase structures and sonata form.

5. **Romanticism (19th century)**: rebelling against Enlightenment reason, it sang of extreme human emotion, fantasy, national myths, and the sublime beauty of nature. Through Schubert's art songs (Lied), the piano virtuosity of Chopin and Liszt, Berlioz's program music (Fantastic Symphony), and Wagner's synthesis of the arts (music drama), the orchestra grew enormously to more than 100 players.

Limitation: Western music history has long been narrated as a hagiographic lineage of great men, centered on European male composers (Bach, Mozart, Beethoven), and modern musicology criticizes this for marginalizing the value of female composers (Clara Schumann, Fanny Mendelssohn) and of non-Western traditional music.

examples.title: An intuitive distinction among monophony, polyphony, and homophony
body: Monophony (single melody): Gregorian chant, in which monks sing only one melody without harmony.
Polyphony (polyphonic music): Bach's fugue, in which four independent melodies intertwine in different rhythms.
Homophony (harmonic music): a Mozart piano sonata, in which the right hand sings an attractive melody while the left hand plays an Alberti bass accompaniment.
Interpretation: These are the three basic textures that show the evolution of the texture (Texture) of Western music.

Step 1: The cello plays the bass line.
Step 2: The harpsichordist reads the figured bass code written in the score and improvises chords to fill in, setting up the pillar of sound.
Interpretation: It is the framework of Baroque music and the core engine of improvised harmonic accompaniment.

mus-14.title: Twentieth-Century Music: Atonality, the Twelve-Tone Technique, and Chance Music
explain: As the chromaticism of late nineteenth-century Romanticism reached its peak, the tonal system centered on the tonic, which had dominated Western music for three hundred years, reached its breaking point. At the turn of the twentieth century, Arnold Schoenberg finally declared the **death of tonality** and founded **atonal music** (Atonality) and the **twelve-tone technique** (Twelve-Tone Technique), into an unexplored realm.

1. **Dissolution of tonality and the twelve-tone technique (dodecaphony)**:
In tonal music, the 'tonic (do)' reigned like a king, and the other notes returned to the tonic, forming a hierarchical society. Schoenberg gave **all twelve semitones within an octave complete democratic equality**. No note should appear more often than the others and form a central pitch (tonality).
- **Prime row (Prime, P)**: a unique series (Row) made by using the twelve semitones once each, without repetition.
- The four transformations of the row: **prime (P)**, **retrograde (Retrograde, R)**, played backward from the end to the beginning; **inversion (Inversion, I)**, which mirrors the intervals up and down like a reflection; and **retrograde-inversion (Retrograde-Inversion, RI)**, which plays the inversion backward. Composers used only these forty-eight row variants as the building material of atonal music, which was mathematically and rigorously controlled.

2. **Impressionism and timbral music**: the French composer Claude Debussy rejected the German functional harmony (T-S-D) and used the **whole-tone scale** (Whole-tone Scale, a scale with no semitones, so its central pitch disappears) and pentatonic scales to capture the faint nuances of waves and light.

3. **John Cage and chance music (Aleatoric Music)**:
The American John Cage turned the definition of music upside down. In <4'33''>, premiered in 1952, the pianist came onstage, closed the piano lid, played not a single note for four minutes and thirty-three seconds while watching the clock, and then exited. What Cage wanted to convey was not silence but the Zen Buddhist realization that **'every accidental sound in the world is music'**, such as the coughing and murmuring of the audience and the rain outside the window, which are heard only in the silence.

Limitation: twelve-tone technique and total serialism (Total Serialism) turned music into a difficult code of sounds that completely alienated the ears of general audiences. As a reaction, in the late 1960s **minimalism** (Minimalism) music, built on the simple rhythmic repetition of Steve Reich and Philip Glass, appeared and won popular response.

examples.title: The retrograde variant of a twelve-tone row
body: Condition: the prime row P begins [C - E - D - F# - ...].
Step 1: The retrograde (R) reads the row backward, from the twelfth and last note toward the first note.
Step 2: It forms a symmetrical structure that perfectly rewinds the time direction of the prime form.
Interpretation: Unity is achieved without any tonal center, through the mathematical network of the twelve tones alone.

body: Condition: the scale [C - D - E - F# - G# - A# - C].
Step 1: Every interval is perfectly uniform, a whole tone (200 cents).
Step 2: Since no semitone (100 cents) exists, the leading-tone pull (semitone attraction) disappears.
Interpretation: Gravity (the tonic) vanishes, creating a dreamlike impressionist atmosphere that seems to float in mid-air.

mus-15.title: Traditional Korean Music: The Twelve Yulryeo, Jeonggan-bo, Sanjo Rhythms, and Tori
explain: Traditional Korean music (gugak, 국악) has an original cosmology and a spatiotemporal formative grammar entirely different from Western music. If Western music is a mechanical beat that divides time and a vertical construction of harmony, gugak is a living music of vitality that revives its tones through **jangdan (장단, 長短), which resembles human breath**, and through **nongheon (농현, 弄絃) and sikimsae (시김새)**, its ornamentation.

1. **The twelve yulryeo (12율려) and the samboon sonik method (三分損益法)**:
The pitch system of gugak consists of twelve pitches (律) built on the base pitch hwangjong (황종, 黃鐘). By dividing the length of a pipe into three equal parts, **samboon-sonil** (三分損一, subtracting one third, a frequency ratio of 3/2 and a perfect fifth upward) and **samboon-ikil** (三分益一, adding one third, a frequency ratio of 4/3 and a perfect fourth downward) are alternated twelve times to produce the twelve pitches. This corresponds mathematically exactly to the fifth-generating method of Pythagorean tuning in ancient Greece.

2. **King Sejong's jeonggan-bo (정간보, 井間譜)**:
The jeonggan-bo, created by King Sejong in the fifteenth century, is the **first quantitative notation in East Asia (유량악보, 有量樂譜)**. A single square cell shaped like the character 井 (jeonggan) stands for 'a fixed unit of time (a beat)', and the names of the pitches (율명, such as hwang, tae, jung, and im) are written inside the cells. An empty cell means that the previous note continues. In this way, not only the pitch but also **'the length of the sound (rhythm)'** can be fully visualized and recorded.

3. **The breath and tempo of sanjo jangdan (장단, 長短)**:
Folk music, p'ansori, and sanjo breathe within the rhythmic frameworks of the janggu drum. Matching the heartbeat and the rise of emotion, they have an **'aesthetics of acceleration'** (가속의 미학), in which the tempo gradually quickens from slow rhythms to fast ones.
- **진양조 (jinyangjo)**: the slowest and most solemn 24-beat rhythm (a four-beat breath of pushing, drawing, closing, and loosening).
- **중모리 (jungmori)**: a lyrical and calm 12-beat rhythm at a moderate tempo.
- **중중모리 (jungjungmori)**: a lively, dancing 12-beat rhythm at a slightly faster tempo.
- **자진모리 (jajinmori)**: an urgent, fast 8-beat rhythm (four beats of three subdivisions each).
- **휘모리 (hwimori)**: the fastest 4-beat rhythm, racing like a storm.

4. **Regional modes: tori (토리)**:
The folk songs and folk music of each region of Korea have distinctive scales and ornamental tones (sikimsae) called 'tori'.
- **남도 육자배기토리 (Namdo yukjabaegi tori)**: from the Jeolla region. In a mi-sol-la-ti-do structure, **'mi is shaken heavily (trembling throat), and ti is bent down from do (bending throat)'**, giving off the sorrow and tragic grandeur of pent-up han (恨).
- **동부 메나리토리 (Dongbu menari tori)**: from the Gangwon and Gyeongsang regions. In a mi-sol-la-do-re mode, a mountain melody with a plaintive descent from la to sol to mi.
- **서도 수심가토리 (Seodo susimga tori)**: from the Hwanghae and Pyeongan regions, a sighing style with nasal (bisung) tones and finely trembling throat.

Limitation: forcibly transplanting gugak onto the five-line Western staff can fade the subtle microtones (quarter tones, 사분음) and the nuances of the flowing and bending sikimsae that are unique to gugak. Therefore, one must acquire its own vocalization (구음, 口音) and breathing.

mus-16.title: Musical Acoustics I: Tuning Systems, the Pythagorean Comma, and Twelve-Tone Equal Temperament
explain: When we play do-re-mi-fa-sol-la-ti on the keys of a piano, is the semitone interval between each key a perfect harmony bestowed by nature? Surprisingly, the twelve semitones of the piano are a **'product of compromise' in which every chord has been deliberately and slightly distorted to hide a mathematical inconsistency**. The keys to solving this dilemma of tuning are the **Pythagorean comma** (Pythagorean Comma) and **equal temperament** (Equal Temperament).

explain.alt: A diagram comparing tuning systems. The errors between just intonation (the integer ratios of the overtones) and twelve-tone equal temperament (100 cents per semitone) are compared. In equal temperament the major third is 14 cents sharp, and the perfect fifth is 2 cents narrow. At the bottom is an explanation of the 23.46-cent Pythagorean comma, the difference between stacking twelve perfect fifths and stacking seven octaves.

explain:
1. **The curse of the Pythagorean comma (Pythagorean Comma)**:
The frequency ratio of the perfect fifth, a perfect consonance, is $3/2$ (1.5), and the frequency ratio of the octave is $2/1$ (2.0).
If you stack twelve perfect fifths one after another, in theory you should pass through all twelve notes and return to the original note seven octaves higher. But let us do the mathematics.
$$(3/2)^{12} \approx 129.746 \quad \text{vs} \quad 2^7 = 128.000$$
두 수치는 일치하지 않는다! $(3/2)^{12} / 2^7 \approx 1.01364$ remains as a subtle gap, and when converted into cents (Cent, 1 semitone = 100 cents, 1 octave = 1200 cents), it becomes **about 23.46 cents**. This is called the **Pythagorean comma**. If you insist on perfect fifths alone, the circle does not close and instead spirals out of alignment.

2. **The blessing and tragedy of just intonation**:
This is a system that tunes using the pure integer ratios of the natural harmonic series (perfect fifth 3/2, major third 5/4). Playing a chord in C major gives a heavenly resonance with no beating, so pure that it almost stings the ear. However, the moment you modulate to D major or F-sharp major by changing the key, the pitch ratios collapse completely, and a terrifying dissonance like a wolf's howl (**wolf interval**, Wolf Interval) bursts out. In just intonation, free modulation is impossible from the start.

3. **The revolutionary compromise of twelve-tone equal temperament (12-TET)**:
This tuning **distributes the 23.5-cent Pythagorean comma thinly and evenly, about 2 cents at a time**, across the twelve semitones. It divides the octave (a ratio of 2) mathematically into twelve equal parts, fixing the frequency ratio of each semitone at $\sqrt[12]{2} \approx 1.05946$. Every semitone is exactly **100 cents**.
- **Cost**: it gives up the perfect harmonic purity of just intonation. The major third of equal temperament (400 cents) is 14 cents sharper (higher) than the just major third (386 cents), so a subtle beating arises.
- **Reward**: since the interval structure is perfectly identical no matter which of the twelve keys you start from, you can **modulate freely into all 24 major and minor keys, without limit**! Johann Sebastian Bach composed the 48 pieces of <The Well-Tempered Clavier> (The Well-Tempered Clavier) to declare the victory of this revolutionary tuning system.

Limitation: unaccompanied choirs (A Cappella) and string quartets are not bound by piano keys, so during performance they momentarily vary their tuning away from twelve-tone equal temperament toward the pure thirds and fifths of just intonation, a 'flexible just tuning' that preserves the purity of chords.

examples.title: Calculating the cents of semitones in twelve-tone equal temperament
body: Condition: one octave is 1200 cents, evenly divided into 12 semitones.
Step 1: One semitone $= 1200 / 12 = 100$ cents.
Step 2: A whole tone (major second) $= 2 \times 100 = 200$ cents. A perfect fifth (7 semitones) $= 7 \times 100 = 700$ cents.
Interpretation: Every interval has a geometric uniformity, falling on an integer multiple of 100.

Step 1: The major third of 12-TET is 400.0 cents.
Interpretation: The major third on a piano is about 14 cents higher than the pure chord, so when two notes are sounded together for a long time, a subtle beating of several cycles per second occurs.

mus-17.title: Musical Acoustics II: The Fourier Harmonic Spectrum and the Timbre of Instruments
explain: Even when a piano, a violin, and a flute play the same A4 note at 440 Hz at the same loudness, we can tell which instrument is which at once, even with our eyes closed. The third sensory property, by which sounds feel different even though their pitch (frequency) and loudness (amplitude) are the same, is called **timbre** (Timbre).

The French mathematician Joseph Fourier proved that every complex periodic sound wave in nature can be completely decomposed into 'a simple sum of a fundamental frequency and numerous sine waves of harmonics' (the Fourier transform). In other words, the physical reason each instrument has its own timbre is that the **kinds of harmonics contained in the sound and the relative energy ratio of each harmonic (harmonic spectrum, Spectral Envelope)** differ from one another.

Sound production mechanisms and harmonic structure of each instrument family:
1. **Strings (violin, cello, guitar)**: when the string is bowed or plucked, the vibration of the string is transmitted through the bridge to the soundboard. All integer-multiple harmonics, from the first harmonic up to the higher ones, are emitted richly, producing the warm and lustrous brilliance characteristic of string instruments.
2. **Open-pipe instruments (flute)**: air vibrates in a pipe open at both ends (Open Pipe). All harmonics, $n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5...$, form evenly, producing a clear and pure sound. Overblowing to the octave is possible.
3. **Closed-pipe instruments (clarinet)**: a pipe closed at one end by the reed mouthpiece (Closed Pipe). By the physics of air-column resonance, the even harmonics cancel out, and **only the odd harmonics ($n = 1, 3, 5, 7...$) are strongly produced**. Because of this unique odd-harmonic structure, the clarinet has a round, somewhat hollow, dark and secluded pastoral timbre.
4. **Brass instruments (trumpet, horn)**: the vibration of the player's lips (Lip-reed) is amplified through the mouthpiece into the bell. The harder one blows, the more the energy of the higher harmonics explodes, emitting a sharp and majestic metallic brilliance.

ADSR envelope (Envelope): timbre depends not only on the static frequency distribution but also on the dynamic shape of how the sound changes over time. The four stages of this trajectory, **Attack (rise time) - Decay (decay) - Sustain (hold) - Release (fade out)**, distinguish the sense of impact of percussion and wind instruments.

Limitation: a pure single-instrument sound sounds dry in an anechoic chamber (Echo-free chamber). The moving timbre we feel in a theater is the result of spatial acoustic resonance created when the sound of the instruments combines with the acoustic reflections of the hall's walls (reverberation).

examples.title: Spectral analysis of the odd harmonics of the clarinet (closed pipe)
body: Condition: the sound played on a clarinet is observed with a frequency spectrum analyzer.
Step 1: Strong energy peaks rise at the positions of the first harmonic (fundamental), the third harmonic, and the fifth harmonic.
Step 2: At the positions of the second and fourth harmonics (even harmonics), there is almost no energy, and they sink to the floor.
Interpretation: The odd-harmonic character of closed-pipe air-column resonance determines the clarinet's own soft and mysterious timbre.

examples.title: Additive synthesis (Additive Synthesis) on a synthesizer
body: Condition: a flute sound is synthesized with an electronic synthesizer.
Step 1: Mathematically add to the sine wave of the fundamental (first harmonic) a sine wave of the second harmonic at 30% and of the third harmonic at 10%.
Step 2: Apply an ADSR envelope with a quick attack and a gently sustained sustain.
Interpretation: Through the principle of superposition of Fourier harmonics, the timbre of a natural instrument is electronically reproduced precisely.

mus-18.title: Music Cognitive Psychology: The Neural Basis of Consonance and Tonal Gravity
explain: Why do we feel peace of mind when we hear certain intervals (the octave and the fifth), and why do we feel instinctive tension and displeasure when we hear others (the semitone and the tritone)? Music is a **neurocognitive-psychological event**, in which sound waves entering through the outer ear are processed in the cochlea and the neural network of the brain.

1. **Neuroacoustic mechanisms of consonance and dissonance (the Helmholtz and Plomp-Levelt models)**:
In the basilar membrane (Basilar Membrane) inside the cochlea, cells that resonate with each frequency are arranged side by side. When two notes sound simultaneously, if the two frequencies are so close that they interfere with each other within the **critical bandwidth (Critical Bandwidth)**, the same neural response zone of the basilar membrane, intense neural friction beating (roughness) occurs, 20 to 40 times per second. The brain perceives this neural friction as the tension and displeasure of **dissonance (Dissonance)**. Conversely, when the frequency ratio forms a simple integer ratio (1:2, 2:3), the harmonics coincide perfectly and the neural friction becomes zero, and this is perceived as **consonance (Consonance)**.

2. **Tonal gravity (Tonal Gravity) and the cognitive mental model**:
The music psychologist Carol Krumhansl demonstrated the **tonal hierarchy (Tonal Hierarchy)**, the hierarchical mental model that the human brain forms when listening to tonal music.
- **Tonic**: the center point with the strongest mass and gravity, like the sun.
- **Leading tone** and dissonant notes possess potential energy displaced from the center. The human brain feels deep emotional catharsis when these tense notes are resolved and fall to the central tonic (gravitational convergence).

3. **Gestalt principles of melodic perception (Leonard Meyer's expectation theory)**:
- **Law of pitch proximity (Pitch Proximity)**: the ear easily hears a stepwise melody that moves by half steps or whole steps as one coherent line.
- **Gap-fill principle (Gap-Fill Principle)**: when a melody leaps greatly (a gap) by an octave or a sixth or more, the brain feels instability and holds a strong psychological expectation to fill the empty space (fill) by moving stepwise downward in the opposite direction.

4. **Minor mode and the evolutionary psychology of sadness**:
The reason major sounds bright and minor sounds sad is linked not only to cultural learning but also to acoustic and linguistic evolution. When humans speak in sadness or despondency, the intonation of the voice falls slightly (on average 30–50 cents flat) and the harmonic components sink. This matches perfectly the interval structure of the minor third in the minor mode.

Limitation: the criteria of consonance shaped by Western classical music are not absolute. In Balinese gamelan music, African polyrhythms, and the microtonal makam culture of the Middle East, dissonances as judged by Western standards are perceived as sources of brilliant energy, so cultural diversity must be respected alongside them.

examples.title: Cognitive analysis of the gap-fill pattern after a melodic leap
body: Condition: in a film theme song, to express the protagonist's resolve, the melody leaps a full octave from the tonic 'do' up to the 'do' an octave higher.
Step 1: A strong tension and a gap form in the brain.
Step 2: The melody then moves stepwise downward in the opposite direction, 'ti-la-sol', filling the empty space.
Interpretation: The excitement of the leap and the stability of the return combine to create a fine melody that perfectly satisfies human expectation.

examples.title: Friction experiment with the critical band (Critical Band)
body: Condition: the notes 440 Hz (A) and 460 Hz are sounded together.
Step 1: Because the frequency difference is only 20 Hz, the two collide violently within the critical band of the basilar membrane.
Step 2: Twenty times per second, neural roughness occurs, giving the listener an instinctive, piercing dissonant discomfort in the ear.
Interpretation: The fear of dissonance is rooted in the physical neural mechanism of the cochlea, which precedes any cultural prejudice.

mus-19.title: Capstone: In-Depth Analysis of the Harmony and Form of a Classical Piece
explain: The culmination of the bachelor's program in musicology is **musical analysis** (Musical Analysis), in which individual theories (functional harmony, non-harmonic tones, counterpoint, sonata form, and acoustics) are applied to the actual text of a score to decode, without missing a single note, the architectural beauty and narrative tension of a piece.

Let us take as the object of analysis a hypothetical short piano sonata in the Classical style (C major, 4/4 time, 32 measures in total).
1. **Formal analysis**: The entire 32 measures make up the whole **exposition** (Exposition) of a typical sonata form. Measures 1–8 form a stately first-theme phrase centered on the tonic chord of C major ($I$), closing with a perfect authentic cadence (PAC) in measure 8. Measures 9–16 are a transition, in which, with the secondary dominant $V^7/V$ accompanied by an F-sharp accidental, a vigorous modulation to G major (the dominant key) is carried out. Measures 17–28 are a graceful and lyrical second-theme phrase settled in G major. Measures 29–32 are a codetta (Codetta) that closes the exposition with a perfect authentic cadence in the dominant key.
2. **Harmonic and non-harmonic-tone analysis**: Just before the cadence in measure 7, a **cadential six-four chord** ($I^6_4$), with do-mi-sol built over the bass sol (G), appears and resolves by a 4-3 descent to the dominant ($V$). In the transition climax of measure 14, the soprano emits an appoggiatura (Appoggiatura), leaping and then descending stepwise, which heightens the tension.
3. **Review of voice leading**: The outer voices (soprano and bass) maintain a thorough contrary motion (Contrary Motion) throughout the move from the first theme to the second theme, and they completely avoid the prohibitions on parallel fifths and parallel octaves.

The ultimate purpose of musical analysis is not merely attaching symbols. By grasping the topography of the harmonic points of tension (tension point) and the resolutions (resolution) in a score, the performer gains a firm scholarly basis for interpretation (Interpretation): where to use a crescendo and where to apply rubato (adjusting the tempo).

examples.title: Decoding the cadential six-four chord in measure 7
body: Score: the bass holds the note sol (G) for two beats, and the right-hand chord moves from do-mi-sol to ti-re-sol.
Step 1: The chord in the first half is C/G, the six-four chord $I^6_4$.
Step 2: In the second half, do descends to ti and mi descends to re, by a half step and a whole step respectively, resolving to the regular $V$ chord.
Interpretation: In Roman numeral analysis it is written $I^6_4 - V$ (or $V^{6-5}_{4-3}$), and it is a typical gesture that prepares the perfect authentic cadence.

examples.title: Measure 14: identifying the modulation and the secondary dominant seventh chord
body: Score: a D7 chord (re-fa#-la-do) with an F-sharp accidental sounds, and the bass resolves to sol (G).
Step 1: C major has no F-sharp, so it is a sign of a temporary or lasting modulation.
Step 2: D7 is the $V^7$ of G major, so its symbol is $V^7 / V$.
Interpretation: With this chord as the turning point, the piece firmly enters the territory of G major, the dominant key.

checks.explanation: The opposition between the first theme in the tonic (I) and the second theme in the dominant (V) is the core grammar of the exposition of sonata form.

checks.hint: It is the six-four chord (I 6/4), in which the bass is the fifth (sol).

checks.hint: It is a secondary dominant seventh chord aiming at the dominant (V).
checks.explanation: Since it is the dominant seventh chord of the G (V) chord, it is written V7/V.

mus-20.title: Capstone: Motivic Arrangement and an Analytical Critique
explain: The final capstone task of the bachelor's program in musicology is to complete a **'four-voice (SATB) functional harmony arrangement and musical analysis critique'** based on a given eight-measure melodic motif. Going beyond analytical passivity, it simultaneously tests active creation, in which one organizes actual notes, avoids voice-leading prohibitions, and builds the key, and scholarly critique.

The standard seven-part frame of the capstone critique is as follows.
1. **Motif melody analysis**: the meter, the scale, and the phrase structure of the given eight-measure melody (the question-and-answer structure of a four-measure phrase plus a four-measure phrase), and the phrasing of the melody
2. **Design of the harmonic progression (Chords)**: the placement of Roman numeral chord symbols by measure, based on the T-S-D functional cycle (I, IV, V, vi, ii6, V7, and so on)
3. **Four-voice (SATB) voice placement and prohibition check**: the placement of the soprano, alto, tenor, and bass, whether the prohibitions on parallel fifths and parallel octaves are avoided, and the design of contrary motion
4. **Non-harmonic tones and ornamental expression**: melodic smoothness and harmonic tension points formed through the placement of passing tones, suspensions (4-3), and appoggiaturas
5. **Cadence (Cadence) design**: building a half cadence (? -> V) at the end of the first four-measure half, and a perfect authentic cadence (V7 -> I) at the final close of the eight measures
6. **Acoustic balance and consideration of timbre (Timbre)**: spacing between voices (soprano-alto and alto-tenor recommended within an octave), and the design of the resonance of the low bass harmonics
7. **Critical self-evaluation**: critique of the musical completeness of the arrangement, adherence to the Classical style, and the possibility of a modern reinterpretation

An excellent four-voice arrangement is one in which all four voices each sing their own independent melodic beauty, yet when they come to rest vertically, they build an airtight pillar of functional harmony.

In the self-evaluation, three points must be checked strictly. (1) Is there any fatal error of parallel fifths or parallel octaves between the bass and the soprano? (2) Do the cadences at measures 4 and 8 provide a clear closure of breath? (3) Do the alto or tenor voices move smoothly, rather than being tediously confined to a single note?

Limitation: this capstone task is not graded automatically. Based on the checklist provided, the learner reviews their own four-voice score and critique from the viewpoint of a composer and a musicologist.

examples.title: An example of designing the harmonic progression of an eight-measure four-voice arrangement
body: Measures 1–2: I - vi - IV - V (the basic T-S-D cycle).
Measures 3–4: I6 - ii6 - V (a half cadence, a question mark that signals the end of the first half).
Measures 5–6: I - V7/V - V - vi (expansion of the narrative through a secondary chord and a deceptive cadence).
Measures 7–8: IV - I6/4 - V7 - I (the cadential six-four and its resolution by a perfect authentic cadence, PAC).
Interpretation: This is a complete Classical period (Period) harmonic structure in which the half cadence and the perfect authentic cadence form a pair.

examples.title: A self-check example of voice-leading prohibitions
body: Condition: check the progression IV -> I6/4 in measure 7.
Step 1: From IV (fa-la-do) to I6/4 (do-mi-sol), the bass fa moves up to sol.
Step 2: If the soprano's do moves up to re, a parallel fifth results, so the soprano should stay on 'do' or move down, avoiding the prohibition by contrary motion.
Interpretation: When connecting harmonies, dynamically cross-check the intervallic relations between the voices.

checks.explanation: This is the classical arrangement process that starts from motif analysis and is completed through four-voice voice leading, a check of the prohibitions, and critique.

Filling in the chord tones of the inner voices (alto, tenor) and checking the prohibitions on parallel fifths and octaves

checks.hint: A half cadence with a question mark is ideal for the end of the first half.
checks.explanation: The standard of the Classical style is to place a half cadence that stays open on V at measure 4, and a perfect authentic cadence that closes on I at the end of measure 8.
options: Half cadence (Half Cadence), which stops on the dominant (V) to lead to the next phrase
Perfect authentic cadence in which all instruments stop playing permanently
Silence in which the sound disappears

Include the key, the T-S-D harmonic progression and cadence types, the measures for avoiding the prohibitions on parallel fifths and octaves, and the placement of non-harmonic tones.

Using active contrary motion in the outer voices, the arrangement fully avoids the prohibitions on parallel fifths and octaves and preserves the independence of each voice. Passing tones and the 4-3 suspension in measure 7 raise the completeness of the melodic tension and its resolution.
